'''Christopher Airay''' (1601 – 18 October 1670) was an English preacher and a pioneer in English logic.

==Life==
Airay was born at [[Clifton, Cumbria|Clifton]] in [[Westmorland|Westmoreland]] in 1600/01. [[Anthony Wood (antiquary)|Anthony Wood]] states that he became a student in [[The Queen's College, Oxford]] and earned a Master of Arts. In 1627 he was elected fellow. About this time he entered into holy orders, according to the statutes of the house, and became a preacher. He was created B.D. in 1642.

Airay was presented to the living of [[Milford, Hampshire]]; where he died on [[St. Luke's Day]], 1670, and was buried in the chancel of his church. His epitaph read:

<blockquote>''Memoriæ sacrum Christopheri Airay, S. T. Bac. olim Coll. Reg. Oxon. socii et hujus ecclesiæ Vicarii vigilantissimi, viri summæ integritatis, judicii acerrimi et ingenii literarum omnium capacis; qui difficillime seculo inter æstuantes rerum fluctus clavum rectum tenuit. Mortalitatem tandem exuit 18 Oct. annos natus 69.''</blockquote>

==Works==
Whilst still at the university he published anonymously his one known book, viz.: ‘Fascicvlvs Præceptorvm Logicorvm in gratiam juventutis academicæ compositus et nunc primum typis donatus. Oxoniæ excudebat Gvlielmus Tvrner Academiæ Typographus. An. D. 1628. Cum Priuilegio’ (pp.&nbsp;224). The printer signs the ‘Præfatio.’ The following are the main headings: Lib. 1, De Prædicabilibus; 2. De Anteprædicamentis; 3, De Propositione; 4. De Demonstratione; 5. De Syllogismo Topico; 6. De Syllogismo Sophistico. Logic is mixed with metaphysics.  A second edition appeared in 1660.
